title: Microbial Biotechnology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Microbial Biotechnology curriculum: recombinant protein production, enzyme technology and immobilisation, monoclonal antibody technology, microbial biosensors, agricultural biotechnology (Bt toxin, biofertilisers), biofuels and bioplastics, and genetically modified organisms -- focused on genetic-engineering-enabled applications, distinct from MCB406's process-engineering focus on industrial fermentation.

questions.question: Recombinant human insulin, one of the earliest and most significant products of microbial biotechnology, is commercially produced by:
options: Extracting insulin directly from pig pancreas only
Inserting the human insulin gene into a microbial host (e.g. Escherichia coli or yeast), which then expresses and produces the human insulin protein
Chemically synthesising insulin atom by atom
Isolating insulin from human blood donors
questions.correct_answer: Inserting the human insulin gene into a microbial host (e.g. Escherichia coli or yeast), which then expresses and produces the human insulin protein
questions.explanation: Recombinant DNA technology allowed the human insulin gene to be cloned into expression vectors and introduced into E. coli or yeast, enabling large-scale microbial fermentation production of authentic human insulin, replacing earlier reliance on animal-extracted insulin.

questions.question: An expression vector used to produce a recombinant protein in a microbial host must include, in addition to the gene of interest:
options: No additional regulatory elements at all
A strong promoter recognised by the host's transcriptional machinery, a ribosome binding site, and appropriate transcription/translation termination signals
Only an origin of replication, with no promoter needed
Human-specific splicing machinery in all cases
questions.correct_answer: A strong promoter recognised by the host's transcriptional machinery, a ribosome binding site, and appropriate transcription/translation termination signals
questions.explanation: For a cloned gene to be efficiently expressed in a microbial host, the expression vector must supply a compatible strong promoter, ribosome binding site (in bacteria), and termination signals recognised by the host's transcription/translation machinery, in addition to the coding sequence itself.

questions.question: Escherichia coli is a widely used host for recombinant protein expression, but a notable limitation for producing complex human therapeutic proteins is that E. coli:
options: Cannot take up any foreign DNA
Lacks the machinery for post-translational modifications such as glycosylation that many human proteins require for full biological activity
Grows too slowly to be useful industrially
Cannot be genetically manipulated at all
questions.correct_answer: Lacks the machinery for post-translational modifications such as glycosylation that many human proteins require for full biological activity
questions.explanation: As a prokaryote, E. coli cannot perform eukaryotic post-translational modifications like glycosylation, disulfide bond formation in the cytoplasm, or complex protein folding assistance; this limits its use for producing certain complex human glycoproteins, for which eukaryotic hosts (yeast, mammalian cell lines) are often preferred.

questions.question: Pichia pastoris, a methylotrophic yeast, is a popular host for recombinant protein production in biotechnology mainly because it:
options: Cannot secrete any proteins

Combines the ease of genetic manipulation and fermentation of a microorganism with eukaryotic post-translational modification capability and efficient secretion of the target protein into the culture medium
Can only be grown in a laboratory setting for a few hours
Requires human cell culture facilities
questions.correct_answer: Combines the ease of genetic manipulation and fermentation of a microorganism with eukaryotic post-translational modification capability and efficient secretion of the target protein into the culture medium
questions.explanation: Pichia pastoris offers the practical advantages of microbial fermentation (fast growth, simple genetics, high cell density, low-cost media) combined with eukaryotic protein processing (folding, some glycosylation) and strong secretion signals, simplifying downstream purification of the target recombinant protein.

questions.question: In enzyme technology, immobilised enzymes (attached to or entrapped within a solid support) offer which key advantage over free (soluble) enzymes in industrial processes?
options: They are always less active than free enzymes
They can typically be reused across multiple batches and easily separated from the product stream, improving process economics and simplifying downstream processing
They cannot be used in continuous processes
They lose all catalytic activity once immobilised
questions.correct_answer: They can typically be reused across multiple batches and easily separated from the product stream, improving process economics and simplifying downstream processing
questions.explanation: Immobilisation (by adsorption, covalent binding, entrapment, or encapsulation) allows enzymes to be physically retained and reused across multiple reaction cycles, and simplifies separating the enzyme from the product stream, often improving process economics and enabling continuous-flow bioreactor operation.

questions.question: Glucose isomerase, an industrially important immobilised enzyme, is used commercially to produce:
options: Penicillin from precursor molecules
High-fructose corn syrup, by converting glucose to the sweeter sugar fructose
Citric acid from molasses
Ethanol from starch
questions.correct_answer: High-fructose corn syrup, by converting glucose to the sweeter sugar fructose
questions.explanation: Immobilised glucose isomerase is used in large-scale continuous reactors to isomerise glucose (from starch hydrolysis) into the sweeter-tasting fructose, a key step in manufacturing high-fructose corn syrup for the food and beverage industry.

questions.question: Restriction enzymes and DNA polymerases used routinely in biotechnology laboratories are themselves examples of:
options: Structural proteins with no catalytic role
Microbially derived enzymes purified and supplied as reagents/tools for molecular biology and genetic engineering applications
Human-derived hormones
Antibiotics
questions.correct_answer: Microbially derived enzymes purified and supplied as reagents/tools for molecular biology and genetic engineering applications
questions.explanation: Restriction endonucleases and many DNA polymerases (e.g. Taq polymerase) are proteins originally purified from microorganisms (often exploiting their natural roles, like restriction-modification systems), now produced and marketed as essential reagent tools underpinning modern biotechnology techniques.

questions.question: Monoclonal antibodies, widely used in diagnostics and therapeutics, are traditionally produced using hybridoma technology, which involves:
options: Fusing an antibody-producing B lymphocyte with an immortal myeloma cell, creating a hybrid cell line that both proliferates indefinitely and secretes a single, defined antibody
Extracting antibodies directly and only from a patient's serum
Growing bacteria that naturally produce human antibodies
Chemically synthesising antibody proteins from amino acids
questions.correct_answer: Fusing an antibody-producing B lymphocyte with an immortal myeloma cell, creating a hybrid cell line that both proliferates indefinitely and secretes a single, defined antibody
questions.explanation: Hybridoma technology, developed by Kohler and Milstein, fuses a short-lived, antibody-secreting B cell with an immortal myeloma cell line; the resulting hybridoma combines indefinite proliferation with the ability to continuously secrete a single, monoclonal (identical) antibody of defined specificity.

questions.question: A key advantage of monoclonal antibodies over polyclonal antisera in diagnostic and therapeutic applications is that monoclonal antibodies:
options: Are a heterogeneous mixture of antibodies recognising many different epitopes
Are highly specific, recognising a single defined epitope, providing greater consistency and reproducibility between batches
Cannot be produced in large, consistent quantities
Are always less specific than polyclonal antisera
questions.correct_answer: Are highly specific, recognising a single defined epitope, providing greater consistency and reproducibility between batches
questions.explanation: Because a monoclonal antibody derives from a single B cell clone, it recognises one specific epitope with defined affinity, giving far greater specificity, consistency, and batch-to-batch reproducibility than polyclonal antisera, which contain a heterogeneous mixture of antibodies against multiple epitopes.

questions.question: A microbial biosensor is best described as a device that combines:
options: A purely mechanical detector with no biological component

A biological recognition element (e.g. whole microorganisms or microbial enzymes) coupled to a transducer, which converts a specific biological/biochemical interaction into a measurable signal (e.g. electrical, optical)
Only chemical reagents with no living component
A microscope used to visually count colonies
questions.correct_answer: A biological recognition element (e.g. whole microorganisms or microbial enzymes) coupled to a transducer, which converts a specific biological/biochemical interaction into a measurable signal (e.g. electrical, optical)
questions.explanation: Microbial biosensors integrate a biological sensing component, such as whole cells engineered to respond to a target analyte or purified microbial enzymes, with a transducer that translates the resulting biochemical change into a quantifiable electrical, optical, or other signal for detection.

questions.question: Whole-cell microbial biosensors engineered with a reporter gene (e.g. green fluorescent protein or lux genes) fused to a promoter that responds to a target pollutant are used to:
options: Produce antibiotics industrially
Detect the presence and relative concentration of the target pollutant in an environmental sample, since exposure activates the promoter and produces a measurable reporter signal
Replace all chemical analytical methods entirely
Sterilise the sample being tested
questions.correct_answer: Detect the presence and relative concentration of the target pollutant in an environmental sample, since exposure activates the promoter and produces a measurable reporter signal
questions.explanation: By linking a pollutant-responsive promoter to a reporter gene, engineered whole-cell biosensors produce a measurable signal (e.g. luminescence or fluorescence) proportional to their exposure to the target compound, allowing relatively rapid, sensitive environmental monitoring of specific contaminants.

questions.question: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is exploited in agricultural biotechnology mainly for its ability to produce:
options: A broad-spectrum antibiotic used in human medicine
Crystal (Cry) proteins that are toxic to specific insect larvae (e.g. certain caterpillars) when ingested, but are generally considered safe for humans and most non-target organisms
Nitrogen-fixing enzymes for soil fertility
A plant growth hormone
questions.correct_answer: Crystal (Cry) proteins that are toxic to specific insect larvae (e.g. certain caterpillars) when ingested, but are generally considered safe for humans and most non-target organisms
questions.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis produces parasporal crystal (Cry) proteins that, once ingested and activated in the alkaline gut of susceptible insect larvae, disrupt the gut epithelium and kill the insect; because activation requires the specific insect gut environment, Bt toxins show considerable target specificity and are widely used in biopesticides and Bt crops.

questions.question: Genetically modified 'Bt crops' (e.g. Bt cotton, Bt maize) have been engineered to:
options: Express the Bacillus thuringiensis Cry toxin gene within the plant's own tissues, conferring built-in resistance to certain insect pests
Produce their own synthetic chemical pesticides unrelated to any microorganism
Eliminate the need for any water during cultivation
Grow without any soil nutrients
questions.correct_answer: Express the Bacillus thuringiensis Cry toxin gene within the plant's own tissues, conferring built-in resistance to certain insect pests
questions.explanation: Bt crops carry a transgene derived from Bacillus thuringiensis encoding a Cry toxin, allowing the plant itself to produce the insecticidal protein in its tissues, reducing the need for external chemical insecticide application against susceptible target pests.

questions.question: Microbial biofertilisers, such as those based on Rhizobium or Azotobacter, improve soil fertility and crop yield mainly by:
options: Killing all other soil microorganisms
Fixing atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can use, or otherwise enhancing nutrient availability (e.g. phosphate solubilisation), reducing dependence on chemical fertilisers
Acting as a herbicide against weeds
Sterilising the soil to prevent plant disease
questions.correct_answer: Fixing atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can use, or otherwise enhancing nutrient availability (e.g. phosphate solubilisation), reducing dependence on chemical fertilisers
questions.explanation: Biofertiliser organisms such as symbiotic Rhizobium (nodulating legume roots) or free-living Azotobacter fix atmospheric nitrogen into plant-available forms, while other biofertiliser microbes solubilise soil phosphate, together improving plant nutrient availability and reducing the need for synthetic chemical fertiliser input.

questions.question: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is exploited as a natural genetic engineering tool in plant biotechnology because it naturally:
options: Cannot transfer any DNA to plant cells
Transfers a defined segment of its Ti (tumour-inducing) plasmid, the T-DNA, into plant cell chromosomes, a mechanism that has been adapted to insert genes of interest into crop plants
Only infects animal cells
Destroys plant DNA upon contact
questions.correct_answer: Transfers a defined segment of its Ti (tumour-inducing) plasmid, the T-DNA, into plant cell chromosomes, a mechanism that has been adapted to insert genes of interest into crop plants
questions.explanation: Agrobacterium tumefaciens naturally causes crown gall disease by transferring T-DNA from its Ti plasmid into the plant genome; biotechnologists have exploited and modified this natural gene-transfer mechanism (replacing the tumour-inducing genes with genes of interest) as a standard method for producing transgenic plants.

questions.question: Bioethanol production from lignocellulosic (plant fibre) biomass, an important area of microbial biofuel research, requires an additional pretreatment/hydrolysis step compared with starch- or sugar-based ethanol production mainly because:
options: Lignocellulose consists of complex, recalcitrant cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin that must first be broken down into fermentable sugars before microorganisms can use them
Lignocellulosic biomass already contains pure glucose ready for fermentation
Yeast can ferment lignin directly with no pretreatment
No enzymes are involved in the process
questions.correct_answer: Lignocellulose consists of complex, recalcitrant cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin that must first be broken down into fermentable sugars before microorganisms can use them
questions.explanation: Unlike starch or sugar feedstocks, lignocellulosic biomass has a complex, rigid structure of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin that is inherently resistant to microbial and enzymatic breakdown, requiring pretreatment (physical/chemical) and enzymatic (e.g. cellulase) hydrolysis to release fermentable sugars before microbial fermentation to ethanol can proceed.

questions.question: Biodiesel can be produced with the aid of microbial lipase enzymes, which catalyse:
options: Fermentation of glucose to ethanol
Transesterification of triglycerides (fats/oils) with an alcohol (e.g. methanol) to produce fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel) and glycerol
Fixation of atmospheric nitrogen
Hydrolysis of cellulose to glucose
questions.correct_answer: Transesterification of triglycerides (fats/oils) with an alcohol (e.g. methanol) to produce fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel) and glycerol
questions.explanation: Microbial (often fungal or bacterial) lipases can catalyse transesterification, converting triglycerides and an alcohol into fatty acid alkyl esters (biodiesel) and glycerol as a byproduct, offering an enzymatic alternative to conventional chemical-catalyst-based biodiesel production.

questions.question: Certain bacteria, such as Cupriavidus necator (formerly Ralstonia eutropha), are of biotechnological interest for their ability to accumulate intracellular granules of:
options: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), biodegradable bioplastic polymers, as an internal carbon/energy storage reserve
Elemental gold
Table salt (sodium chloride) crystals
Pure cellulose fibres
questions.correct_answer: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), biodegradable bioplastic polymers, as an internal carbon/energy storage reserve
questions.explanation: Under nutrient-limited conditions with excess carbon, certain bacteria accumulate polyhydroxyalkanoates as intracellular storage granules; because PHA is biodegradable and has plastic-like properties, these bacteria are cultivated industrially to produce PHA as an environmentally friendly alternative to petroleum-based plastics.

questions.question: A major advantage claimed for microbially produced bioplastics such as PHA, compared with conventional petroleum-based plastics, is that PHA:
options: Is completely non-biodegradable, lasting indefinitely in the environment
Is biodegradable by many environmental microorganisms, breaking down into water and carbon dioxide under suitable conditions
Can only be produced from crude oil
Has no practical commercial applications
questions.correct_answer: Is biodegradable by many environmental microorganisms, breaking down into water and carbon dioxide under suitable conditions
questions.explanation: Unlike most conventional plastics, PHA and related bioplastics can be enzymatically degraded by a range of environmental microorganisms into simple, harmless end products such as CO2 and water, making them attractive as more environmentally sustainable plastic alternatives.

questions.question: A genetically modified organism (GMO), as used in biotechnology, is defined as an organism whose:
options: Genetic material has been altered using genetic engineering techniques in a way that does not occur naturally through mating or natural recombination
Phenotype has changed due to environmental factors alone, with no change to its DNA
Species classification has changed due to evolution over many generations
Genome is identical to its wild-type ancestor
questions.correct_answer: Genetic material has been altered using genetic engineering techniques in a way that does not occur naturally through mating or natural recombination
questions.explanation: A GMO's genome has been deliberately modified using recombinant DNA or other genetic engineering techniques (e.g. introducing a foreign gene, deleting/altering a native gene) in ways that would not typically occur through natural mating or recombination processes alone.

questions.question: Biosafety and regulatory risk assessment of genetically modified microorganisms intended for environmental release (e.g. an engineered biofertiliser strain) typically evaluates:
options: Only the organism's colour and smell
Potential risks such as unintended gene transfer to other organisms, survival and persistence in the environment, and possible ecological impact on non-target species
Nothing, since GMOs are automatically considered completely safe
Only the manufacturing cost of the organism
questions.correct_answer: Potential risks such as unintended gene transfer to other organisms, survival and persistence in the environment, and possible ecological impact on non-target species
questions.explanation: Biosafety risk assessment for environmentally released GMOs considers factors such as the likelihood of horizontal gene transfer to wild-type organisms, the modified organism's ability to survive and spread in the environment, and any potential adverse effects on non-target species or ecosystems, informing regulatory approval decisions.

questions.question: A selectable marker gene, such as an antibiotic resistance gene, is commonly included in a genetic engineering construct mainly to:
options: Increase the size of the plasmid without any functional purpose
Allow researchers to identify and select only the cells that have successfully taken up and are maintaining the recombinant DNA construct, by growing cultures on selective medium
Directly confer the desired trait being engineered, with no other role
Prevent the vector from replicating
questions.correct_answer: Allow researchers to identify and select only the cells that have successfully taken up and are maintaining the recombinant DNA construct, by growing cultures on selective medium
questions.explanation: Because transformation efficiency is never 100%, a selectable marker (often an antibiotic resistance gene) lets researchers grow the transformed population on medium containing the selective agent, so only cells carrying the recombinant construct (and its associated resistance) survive and grow, distinguishing them from untransformed cells.

questions.question: Protein purification of a recombinant protein tagged with a polyhistidine (His) tag commonly uses which chromatographic technique for efficient, selective isolation?
options: Immobilised metal affinity chromatography (IMAC), exploiting the histidine tag's affinity for immobilised metal ions such as nickel
Simple filtration through cotton wool
Gas chromatography
Paper chromatography
questions.correct_answer: Immobilised metal affinity chromatography (IMAC), exploiting the histidine tag's affinity for immobilised metal ions such as nickel
questions.explanation: A His-tag binds with high affinity to immobilised divalent metal ions (commonly Ni2+ or Co2+) on an IMAC resin; the tagged recombinant protein is selectively retained while other cellular proteins pass through, and is subsequently eluted (often with imidazole), providing an efficient one-step purification approach widely used in biotechnology.

questions.question: Site-directed mutagenesis, a technique used in protein engineering, allows researchers to:
options: Randomly mutate an entire genome with no control over location
Introduce a specific, precisely targeted change (e.g. a single amino acid substitution) at a chosen position within a cloned gene, to study or improve the encoded protein's properties
Delete an organism's entire chromosome
Fuse two unrelated organisms into one cell
questions.correct_answer: Introduce a specific, precisely targeted change (e.g. a single amino acid substitution) at a chosen position within a cloned gene, to study or improve the encoded protein's properties
questions.explanation: Site-directed mutagenesis uses designed oligonucleotide primers carrying the desired base change(s) to introduce a precise, targeted mutation at a specific position in a cloned gene, enabling researchers to study structure-function relationships or engineer improved protein properties (e.g. altered stability, activity, or specificity).

questions.question: Directed evolution, an approach used in enzyme/protein engineering, improves a desired protein property by:
options: Rationally designing the exact final sequence based purely on computational prediction, with no experimental screening

Generating a library of gene variants (via random mutagenesis or recombination), then screening or selecting for improved variants over iterative rounds, mimicking natural evolution under artificial selection pressure
Simply purifying the wild-type protein without any modification
Deleting the gene of interest entirely
questions.correct_answer: Generating a library of gene variants (via random mutagenesis or recombination), then screening or selecting for improved variants over iterative rounds, mimicking natural evolution under artificial selection pressure
questions.explanation: Directed evolution applies iterative cycles of diversification (random mutagenesis, gene shuffling) and screening/selection for a desired property, progressively enriching for improved variants without requiring detailed prior structural knowledge, in a laboratory-accelerated analogue of natural evolution.

questions.question: Microbial production of citric acid, industrially significant in the food and beverage sector, is achieved at large scale predominantly using:
options: Aspergillus niger fermentation of a sugar-rich substrate (e.g. molasses)
Genetically engineered mammalian cell culture
Direct chemical synthesis from petroleum
Extraction from citrus fruit peel exclusively at industrial scale
questions.correct_answer: Aspergillus niger fermentation of a sugar-rich substrate (e.g. molasses)
questions.explanation: Industrial citric acid production overwhelmingly relies on submerged fermentation of a sugar-rich substrate (commonly molasses) by selected high-yielding strains of Aspergillus niger, which has long since displaced extraction from citrus fruit as the dominant commercial production method.

questions.question: Recombinant vaccines, such as the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) vaccine, are produced by:
options: Attenuating the live hepatitis B virus for direct use
Cloning the gene encoding the viral surface antigen into a microbial or yeast host, which then expresses the antigen protein alone (without any complete infectious virus) for use as a subunit vaccine
Extracting the antigen directly from infected human blood, as the only production method
Chemically synthesising the entire viral genome
questions.correct_answer: Cloning the gene encoding the viral surface antigen into a microbial or yeast host, which then expresses the antigen protein alone (without any complete infectious virus) for use as a subunit vaccine
questions.explanation: The hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) vaccine is a classic recombinant subunit vaccine: the HBsAg gene is cloned into a yeast expression system, which produces the antigen protein in large quantities without generating any infectious viral particles, avoiding the safety concerns of using live or blood-derived antigen.

questions.question: Metabolic engineering, as applied in industrial microbial biotechnology, involves:
options: Randomly selecting naturally occurring strains with no genetic modification
Deliberately modifying a microorganism's metabolic pathways (e.g. by overexpressing, deleting, or introducing genes) to redirect metabolic flux toward increased production of a desired compound
Physically removing all enzymes from a cell
Growing cells only in the absence of any carbon source
questions.correct_answer: Deliberately modifying a microorganism's metabolic pathways (e.g. by overexpressing, deleting, or introducing genes) to redirect metabolic flux toward increased production of a desired compound
questions.explanation: Metabolic engineering rationally modifies a host's biochemical pathways, such as amplifying a rate-limiting enzyme, removing a competing pathway, or introducing a heterologous pathway, in order to increase the yield or introduce entirely new production capability for a target metabolite or product.

questions.question: Synthetic biology, an emerging extension of microbial biotechnology, is distinguished from classical genetic engineering mainly by its emphasis on:
options: Using only naturally occurring, unmodified genes
Designing and constructing standardised, modular biological parts and circuits (often using engineering principles) to build organisms with new or enhanced functions in a rational, systematic way
Avoiding any use of DNA sequencing or synthesis technology
Restricting work exclusively to eukaryotic cells
questions.correct_answer: Designing and constructing standardised, modular biological parts and circuits (often using engineering principles) to build organisms with new or enhanced functions in a rational, systematic way
questions.explanation: Synthetic biology extends genetic engineering by applying formal engineering principles -- standardisation, modularity, and abstraction of biological 'parts' (promoters, genes, regulatory circuits) -- to design and build organisms or biological systems with new or improved functions in a more systematic, predictable way.

questions.question: Codon optimisation of a heterologous gene before expressing it in a microbial host is often necessary because:
options: All organisms use an identical set of preferred codons, so this step is never needed
Different organisms show different preferences (codon usage bias) among synonymous codons, and using rare host codons for a foreign gene can slow translation or reduce protein yield
Codon optimisation changes the amino acid sequence of the resulting protein
It is required only for genes shorter than 10 base pairs
questions.correct_answer: Different organisms show different preferences (codon usage bias) among synonymous codons, and using rare host codons for a foreign gene can slow translation or reduce protein yield
questions.explanation: Because synonymous codons are used with different frequencies in different organisms, a foreign gene rich in codons that are rare in the host's tRNA pool can be translated slowly or inefficiently; codon optimisation substitutes synonymous, host-preferred codons (without changing the encoded amino acid sequence) to improve expression levels.

questions.question: A fusion protein tag such as glutathione S-transferase (GST) or maltose-binding protein (MBP), attached to a recombinant target protein, can serve which purpose in biotechnology?
options: It has no practical use and is only a laboratory artefact
It can aid affinity purification and, in some cases, improve the solubility and stability of the fused target protein during expression
It always destroys the biological activity of the target protein
It prevents the protein from being expressed at all
questions.correct_answer: It can aid affinity purification and, in some cases, improve the solubility and stability of the fused target protein during expression
questions.explanation: Fusion tags like GST or MBP can be exploited for affinity-based purification (binding a specific resin) and often improve the solubility/folding of an otherwise poorly soluble target protein when expressed in a heterologous host, after which the tag can typically be removed by a specific protease cleavage site.

questions.question: Bioprospecting for novel microbial enzymes with industrial biotechnology potential (e.g. extremozymes from extremophiles) is valuable because such enzymes can offer:
options: No advantage over conventional mesophilic enzymes
Enhanced stability and activity under industrially relevant extreme conditions (e.g. high temperature, high salinity, extreme pH) that would denature typical mesophilic enzymes
The ability to function only at very low temperatures
Guaranteed toxicity to humans
questions.correct_answer: Enhanced stability and activity under industrially relevant extreme conditions (e.g. high temperature, high salinity, extreme pH) that would denature typical mesophilic enzymes
questions.explanation: Extremozymes from extremophilic microorganisms (thermophiles, halophiles, acidophiles/alkaliphiles) have often evolved structural adaptations that let them remain stable and active under the harsh conditions found in many industrial processes, making them attractive alternatives to conventional enzymes that would denature under the same conditions.
